conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Claire, a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, and it helps us understand what kind of support might be most helpful to you in this postpartum period.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you give permission to share, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to begin?

**Question 1**  
Thinking back over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I have laughed a little, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because anything really feels funny inside. Most of the time I’m just too tired to find much amusing.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can laugh sometimes, but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. A lot of the time I feel too tired or pre-occupied with the baby to really find things funny, even when I know they’re supposed to be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes I do look forward to little things—like when my mom’s coming over to hold the baby so I can shower without rushing—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. Mostly I’m just hoping I’ll have enough energy to enjoy whatever it is, and even then there’s this low-level worry in the back of my mind about whether the baby will be okay while I’m doing it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I catch myself doing that. Like, if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him, I’ll think maybe I missed some cue or didn’t feed him right, even when my head knows babies just cry. It’s not every hour or anything, but I do go down that “what did I do wrong?” rabbit hole more than I should.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… I’ll be sitting there with the baby sleeping soundly and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet, or I start imagining he might stop breathing. Nothing’s actually wrong, but the worry just pops up out of nowhere. It happens a few times a day and makes it hard to relax even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had that full “panic attack” feeling, but sometimes when I’m alone with the baby at night my chest gets tight and I feel this rush of fear, like I’m suddenly sure something awful is about to happen even though I can’t name what. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Some days it feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, trying to nap—there’s another pile of laundry or dishes or a text I forgot to answer, and I just think, “I can’t keep up.” I’m managing, but I’m running on empty and it feels like I’m barely staying ahead.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy” keeping me awake—more like my mind won’t shut off. I lie down and start replaying every little thing I did with the baby, worrying I didn’t burp him long enough or that I missed his tired cues. Even when he’s sleeping, I’m listening for him, so I only drift in short spurts. It’s been several nights this week that I’ve spent more time staring at the ceiling than actually sleeping.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some of the time. It’s not all day, but there are stretches—especially in the late afternoon when I’m really tired—where I just feel weepy and low, like I’m stuck under a gray cloud. It usually lifts a bit when my partner gets home, but while it’s there it feels pretty heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week, but not every day. It’s usually when everything piles up—like yesterday when the baby wouldn’t nap and I spilled the pumped milk. I sat on the floor and tears just came for a minute, then I wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen (EPDS-equivalent)

<sym>Symptoms/behaviors endorsed</sym>
- Reduced ability to laugh/find pleasure (Q1, Q2)
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, “gray cloud” feeling, multiple crying episodes this week (Q8, Q9)
- Excessive self-blame/guilt over routine infant care (Q3)
- Recurrent, intrusive worries (infant safety) and episodic panic-like sensations (tight chest, racing heart) without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)
- Sleep disturbance driven by rumination and hyper-vigilance for infant (Q7)
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “running on empty” (Q6)

<med>Pattern</med>: Depressed mood + anhedonia + guilt + anxiety/arousal symptoms + functional sleep impact = elevated likelihood for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features.

<med>Risk factors noted</med>
- Daily low mood, intermittent crying
- Loss of enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities
- Cognitions of inadequacy/self-blame
- Anxiety spikes and nocturnal panic sensations
- Sleep deprivation secondary to mood rather than solely infant demands

<med>Safety</med>
Denies any self-harm ideation; no current safety concern.

<med>Summary</sym>
Screening responses indicate clinically significant mood and anxiety symptoms consistent with probable postpartum depression (with anxious presentation). Recommend formal diagnostic evaluation and discussion of support/intervention options.
